content: 1. The validation of hepatitis B elimination and the path to its elimination are guided by consolidated guidelines focusing on person-centered viral hepatitis strategic information. These guidelines emphasize the use of data to support the scaling up of hepatitis prevention, diagnosis, and treatment services at the country level. 2. The indicator measuring the coverage of the third dose of the hepatitis B vaccine among infants evaluates the proportion of children under 12 months of age who have received this dose. This indicator is critical for monitoring and guiding immunization programs as recommended by WHO and UNICEF. It is also part of the WHO global reference list of 100 core health indicators, which includes immunization coverage rates for each vaccine in national schedules. 3. This indicator also tracks programmatic targets for validating the elimination of mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B virus (HBV) and the progress toward eliminating hepatitis B as a public health threat. 4. Disaggregation of data by age, place of residence, sex, and socioeconomic status is essential for understanding disparities in vaccine coverage. Global reporting platforms, such as the WHO/UNICEF Joint Reporting Form on Immunization, are used to collect and validate this data. 5. The coverage of HBV testing among pregnant women is another critical indicator. It measures the proportion of pregnant women tested for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) during pregnancy. Testing is vital for the health of the mother and is the first step in preventing mother-to-child transmission of HBV. 6. This indicator informs programs about the interventions needed to strengthen the elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HBV and the need to monitor exposed infants. It also contributes to quality assessments of antenatal care services and tracks programmatic targets for validating HBV elimination. 7. Global targets aim for at least 90% coverage of antenatal testing for HBsAg among pregnant women. Data sources include patient monitoring tools, such as hepatitis and HIV testing service records, lab registers, and antenatal care registers. National program records aggregated from health facility data are ideal, but sentinel surveillance or special studies can also be used. 8. The coverage of antiviral therapy among eligible HBsAg-positive pregnant women measures the proportion of these women who receive antiviral drugs for prophylaxis or treatment according to national policies and WHO guidelines. This indicator reflects sustained service quality throughout antenatal care. 9. Antiviral therapy coverage is a key measure for validating the elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HBV and the progress toward eliminating hepatitis B as a public health threat. Global targets aim for at least 90% coverage with antiviral drugs for eligible HBsAg-positive pregnant women. 10. Data sources for this indicator include program or clinical patient monitoring tools, such as electronic or paper medical records, maternity and antenatal care registers. National program records aggregated from health facility data are preferred, but sentinel surveillance or special studies can be used if necessary. 11. The coverage of hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) among exposed newborns measures the proportion of these infants who receive HBIG according to national policies and WHO guidelines. This indicator is essential for monitoring programmatic targets for eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HBV. 12. Data sources for this indicator include program or clinical patient monitoring tools, such as electronic or paper medical records, maternity and antenatal care registers. National program records aggregated from health facility data are ideal, but sentinel surveillance or special studies can also be used. 13. The number of needles and syringes distributed per person who injects drugs per year is an indicator of progress in improving the coverage of sterile injecting equipment. This is a critical prevention service for people who inject drugs. 14. Needle and syringe programs (NSPs) are essential health sector interventions included in the WHO comprehensive package for HIV prevention and treatment among key populations. These programs also significantly enhance hepatitis prevention for people who inject drugs. 15. At the population level, this indicator measures the total number of sterile injecting equipment units in circulation among people who inject drugs. At the program level, it measures the average number of needles and syringes provided to individuals accessing NSPs. 16. Global targets aim for at least 300 syringes and needles distributed per person who injects drugs per year. Data sources include program data on the number of needles and syringes distributed and estimates of the population size of people who inject drugs. 17. The coverage of opioid agonist maintenance therapy (OAMT) among people who inject drugs measures the percentage of opioid-dependent individuals receiving this therapy. This indicator reflects a program's ability to deliver OAMT as a method of reducing injecting frequency and supporting harm-reduction services. 18. OAMT is a critical intervention for treating opioid dependence and reducing injecting frequency. It also supports the treatment of other health conditions, such as HIV, tuberculosis, and viral hepatitis. 19. Global targets aim for at least 40% of opioid-dependent people who inject drugs to receive OAMT. Data sources include program records, such as OAMT registries, and size estimations of opioid-dependent people who inject drugs. 20. Disaggregation of data by gender, age, and provider type (e.g., key population-led organizations, public sector providers) is essential for understanding disparities in access to OAMT.
